context: The complexity class QMA(2) The power of QMA(2) is not sensitive to the number of separable partitions: [HM13] showed that QMA(2) = QMA(k) for k at most polynomial in n using a primitive called the product test. One reason to believe that QMA(2) is powerful is that QMA(2) can decide NP using only logarithmic-sized proofs [BT12]; by contrast, QMA with logarithmic-sized proofs is equal to BQP. However, since the QMA(2) protocol has a subconstant promise gap, it cannot (so far) be scaled to NEXP [CD10, CF11, ABDFS09, Per12, GNN12]. If there exist efficient algorithms that “disentangle” quantum states, then QMA = QMA(2); [ABDFS09, AKT24] show some evidence that no “disentanglers” exist. Although QMA+ = QMA+ (2) = NEXP [JW23, BFM24], there exist + constants c, s where QMA+ c,s ⊆ QMA and QMA (2)c,s ⊆ QMA(2). In fact, there exists a promise gap + for QMA (2) where a sharp transition in complexity occurs (assuming there is a transition) [JW24]; it is unknown if the same is true for QMA+ . Concurrent work [AGIMR24] simultaneously and independently study the power of QMA with noncollapsing measurements. They show that this computational model is equal to NEXP, also resolving Question 1. However, their proof uses O(n log n) non-collapsing measurements, as opposed to just one in this work. They also explore the power of DQP [Aar05b] in the contexts of quantum verification and quantum advice. Note that one must make minor adjustments to the definitions of CQP and naCQP [ABFL16] to allow non-collapsing measurement on a quantum witness. When c, s are not specified, c−s is allowed to be at least any inverse polynomial in input size. In general, the promise gap can be amplified via parallel repetition or with more clever methods [MW05, NWZ09]. Definition 6 (QMAc,s ). Let c, s : N → R+ be polynomial-time computable functions. A promise problem Lyes , Lno ⊆ {0, 1}∗ is in QMAc,s if there exists a BQP verifier V such that for every n ∈ N and every x ∈ {0, 1}n : • Completeness: if x ∈ Lyes , then there exists a state |ψ⟩ on poly(n) qubits, s.t. Pr[V (x, |ψ⟩) accepts] ≥ c(n) . • Soundness: If x ∈ Lno , then for every state |ψ⟩ on poly(n) qubits, we have Pr[V (x, |ψ⟩) accepts] ≤ s(n) . We prove Theorem 3 using the NEXP-complete problem proposed by [JW23]. Definition 7 (CSP system). A (N, R, q, Σ)-CSP system C on N variables with values in Σ consists of a set (possibly a multi-set) of R constraints where the arity of each constraint is exactly q. Definition 8 (Value of CSP). The value of a (N, R, q, Σ)-CSP system C is the maximum fraction of satisfiable constraints over all possible assignments σ : [N ] → Σ. The value of C is denoted val(C). Definition 9 (GapCSP). The (1, δ)-GapCSP problem takes as input a (N, R, q, Σ)-CSP system C. The task is to distinguish whether C is such that (in completeness) val(C) = 1 or (in soundness) val(C) ≤ δ. Theorem 10 ([JW23]). There exist constants q and δ < 1 and a family of succinct (Ni , Ri , q, Σ = {0, 1})-CSP systems {Ci }i≥1 for which the (1, δ)-GapCSP problem is NEXP-complete. paper_title: Superposition detection and QMA with non-collapsing measurements
statement: 1. Non-collapsing measurement is especially powerful with access to an inefficient quantum state: QMA with non-collapsing measurements equals NEXP, but QCMA with non-collapsing measurements is in PSPACE. Can one use this concept to construct a classical oracle separating QMA and QCMA? Similarly, how does the power of CQP/poly compare to the power of CQP/qpoly = ALL [Aar18]? 2. The position of the non-collapsing measurement in a quantum computation seems to matter in Corollary 4: non-collapsing measurement is used after a collapsing partial measurement. This stymies one approach to prove QMA(2) = NEXP; see discussion in Section 4.2. What is the power of BQP (or QMA) with the ability to make non-collapsing measurements, but only before all collapsing measurements?
